note: Beatrice died in 1290 and the journey is set in 1300. Dante has not seen her face for ten years, and the thirst is simply to look at her.
The old snare of love. Her smile catches him now exactly as it did when she was alive.

context: Faith, hope and love, standing to Dante's left. They break his stare: even here, he must not lose himself in looking at Beatrice. There is a lesson he has to watch first.

note: The procession of Canto 29: the candlesticks, the twenty-four elders, the chariot and those who follow it. It now turns to the right and heads back east, into the sun.
The seven golden candlesticks at the head of the procession, usually read as the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.
The triumphal chariot that carried Beatrice, usually read as the Church. The rest of the canto shows what becomes of it.
The seven virtues: the three theological virtues at the right wheel and the four cardinal virtues at the left.

context: It pulls the chariot without ruffling a feather: Christ guides the Church without effort and without change in himself.
She drew Dante through Lethe in Canto 31. She is still unnamed.
He has walked with Dante since Canto 21 and has been silent since they entered the garden. His penance is done, and he is on his way to Heaven.

note: The right wheel. The chariot is turning to the right, so the wheel on the inside of the turn traces the tighter curve.

context: The garden has stood empty of people since Adam and Eve were driven out.
The whole company murmurs his name in reproach as they reach the tree he ate from.

note: The tree of the knowledge of good and evil, whose fruit God forbade to Adam and Eve (Genesis 2–3). It has been bare since they ate. In the next canto Beatrice makes it a sign of God's justice, and many readers also see in it the Empire, which for Dante was God's instrument of justice on earth.

quote: spreading wider as it climbed higher
note: The opposite of an ordinary tree, so that no one can climb it. The trees on the terrace of the gluttons had the same shape (Purgatorio 22). Beatrice explains it in Canto 33.
The trees of India were a byword for height. Virgil says in the Georgics that no arrow can reach their tops.
Praise for Christ, who was obedient where Adam was not and took nothing from the tree. Many readers also hear Dante's politics: Christ claimed no earthly power, and left the Empire what was its own.

quote: Thus the seed of all justice is preserved
note: The only words the griffin speaks. They recall Christ's words at his baptism: "thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all justice" (Matthew 3:15).

The chariot's shaft, usually read as the cross. A medieval legend held that the cross was made of wood from the tree of knowledge, so in binding the pole to the tree Christ returns to it "what was his own".
Widowed of its leaves and flowers since Adam's sin.
The constellation Pisces. The light that shines after it is Aries, the Ram, the next sign of the zodiac. When the sun is in Aries it is spring, and the trees bud.
A color between rose and violet, often read as the color of Christ's blood. The dead tree flowers the moment the cross touches it: Christ's sacrifice restores what Adam's sin had stripped.

context: The eyes are pitiless because they kept watch over Io without rest. Their watching "cost so dearly" because Mercury killed Argus once they closed.

note: The tale Mercury told to put Argus to sleep, in Ovid's Metamorphoses. Syrinx was a nymph who fled the god Pan and was changed into reeds, from which Pan made his pipes.

context: The comparison is to the Transfiguration (Matthew 17). On a mountain, three disciples saw Christ shining like the sun, with Moses and Elijah beside him. They fell down in terror, and when he touched them and told them to rise, they saw only Jesus, looking as he always had.

note: Christ. The image is from the Song of Songs (2:3): "As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved." At the Transfiguration the disciples saw only its blossom, a glimpse of his glory. The fruit is the full sight of him that feeds the angels in Heaven.
The sleep of death. Christ's word called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised the daughter of Jairus.
The griffin and most of the procession return to Heaven, as Christ ascended after the Resurrection and left his Church on earth.

quote: She sat alone upon the earth itself
note: Beatrice is left to guard the chariot, seated on the bare ground. If the chariot is the Church, she is the divine wisdom that watches over it, and the bare earth is the poverty and humility of its first days.
The four cardinal and three theological virtues. The lights they hold are the seven candlesticks, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which no wind can blow out.
A dweller in this wood. "Here" may mean the garden, where Dante's stay will be short, or the earth, where the rest of his life will be.

quote: that Rome where Christ is Roman
note: Heaven, the true eternal city. It is a measure of what Rome meant to Dante that he can call paradise a Rome and Christ its citizen. Beatrice is promising him salvation.

The order given to John at the start of Revelation: "What you see, write in a book" (1:11). Dante is being made a prophet, and the poem is the book. What follows is a history of the Church in seven scenes, told in the manner of John's visions.
The eagle, bird of Jupiter and emblem of the Roman Empire. Its first attack is the persecution of the early Christians by the Roman emperors.
Heresy, which troubled the Church in its first centuries. It is starved because false teaching has no nourishment in it. Beatrice drives it off, as true doctrine refutes false.

The Donation of Constantine. The Middle Ages believed that the emperor Constantine, in the fourth century, gave the pope rule over Rome and the western empire. The document was a forgery, as was shown in the fifteenth century. Dante thought it real, and a disaster: the gift of wealth and power that began the Church's corruption (Inferno 19).
Usually taken as the voice of Saint Peter. The Church is traditionally the boat of Peter the fisherman, and Constantine's gift is a cargo it was never meant to carry.

The hardest of the seven scenes to pin down. The dragon comes from Revelation 12, where it is Satan. What it tears away is usually read as a great schism in the Church, and many commentators think of the rise of Islam, which medieval Christians saw as a breaking away from Christianity.

quote: covered itself again with the feathers
note: More gifts of land and power to the Church from later rulers. Dante allows that the givers may have meant well. The result is that the whole chariot is smothered in the eagle's plumage, the Church in worldly wealth.
Seven heads and ten horns: the beast of Revelation 17. The chariot of the Church has turned into the monster of the Bible's last book. The seven heads are often read as the seven deadly sins.

The whore of Babylon, who in Revelation 17 sits on the beast and sins with the kings of the earth. She takes the place Beatrice held on the chariot. Dante means the corrupt papacy of his own time, under Boniface VIII and Clement V. He used the same image against the popes in Inferno 19.
The kings of France, and above all Philip IV, called the Fair, who reigned from 1285 to 1314 and bent the papacy to his will.

Why her glance at Dante earns her a beating is not clear. He may stand here for the Christian people, or for Italy. The scourging is usually linked to 1303, when Philip's men seized and humiliated Pope Boniface VIII at Anagni (Purgatorio 20).

In 1309 the French pope Clement V settled the papal court at Avignon, in the south of France, under the eye of the French king. It stayed there until 1377. Dante wrote this after the move, but his journey is set in 1300, so it comes as a vision of the future.
